newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's may ask Names to put more capital up front.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's may ask Names to put more capital up front.

text.p: Lloyd's of London is considering asking investors with unlimited liability to put more capital up front as part of moves to strengthen its financial security.

Senior Lloyd's sources told Reuters on Friday it was possible that Names -- as the individual investors with unlimited liability are called -- may in the future be required to increase funds held at the insurance market to more than the 25 to 30 percent of underwriting risk currently demanded of them.
Such a proposal would, however, not be implemented for the 1997 year and would in any event likely be phased in gradually.

Senior management have also reaffirmed a commitment to retaining Lloyd's "central" fund, which as a last resort guarantees payment of claims in the event one of its insurance syndicates goes out of business or members fail to pay bills.

This decision and possible changes to the overall structure of Lloyd's financial security system come amid fierce debate over the future of the insurance market's central fund and a struggle for influence between Names and corporate investors.

A few of the corporate investors, who first joined Lloyd's in 1994 and several of whom have been aligning more closely with underwriting agents in the insurance market, have questioned the need for the central fund in the future.

They say consolidation among the market's syndicates and underwriting agents may reach a point where Lloyd's comprises several small to medium-sized insurance companies. These would need individual operating licences, not a common Lloyd's one.

Lloyd's wants to keep the central fund, which it feels underpins its whole existence by providing a common security. The fund forms an essential part of the structure which allows member syndicates to sell Lloyd's policies globally.
But while the central fund will continue to exist, it will probably be less often used following the insurance market's return to profit for 1993 after five years of record losses.
Moreover, net resources have increased to 4.7 billion pounds, or 66 percent of liabilities, following completion of Lloyd's recovery plan in September, insurance market sources said.
The central fund was drawn on heavily when many Names were unable or refused to meet cash calls for the eight billion pounds plus of losses suffered by Lloyd's from 1988 to 1992.

It is in part because of this that Lloyd's may ask unlimited liability Names to pledge more capital up front, reducing reliance on personal wealth -- the last layer of security above the central fund. Contributions to the central fund from Names and corporate capital may also be brought more into line.

With published proposals to impose new rules next year on the limited liability corporate funds, under which those with more concentrated exposure would provide more capital under an existing risk-based system, these changes would reduce further the likelihood of Lloyd's having to use its central fund.

Names are still the majority investors in Lloyd's, but are declining in number. They provided 70 percent and corporate members 30 percent of this year's 9.9 billion pounds "capacity" -- the amount Lloyd's can underwrite in terms of premium income.

But Lloyd's estimates that this ratio next year will be about 60:40 and Syndicate Underwriting Research Limited (SURL), owned by Anton Jardine members' agency, has gone further by suggesting corporate investors will provide about 45 percent in 1997.
The Names could become a minority by 1998, possibly leaving them less influential in Lloyd's decision making processes.
